Abstract
Purpose  Laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG) is an effective treatment for obesity, but early weight loss outcomes vary 
owing to individual nutritional and metabolic differences. We developed a nomogram model to predict early weight loss 
after LSG, incorporating computed tomography (CT)-based body composition metrics and preoperative inflammatory-
nutritional markers.
Methods  We retrospectively analyzed 305 patients with obesity who underwent LSG at the Affiliated Hospital of Qingdao 
University between January 2016 and June 2023. An external validation cohort of 105 patients from a separate institution was 
also included. Patients were categorized into optimal remission (%total weight loss [%TWL] ≥ 25%) and suboptimal remis-
sion (%TWL < 25%) weight loss groups one year postoperatively. Predictive variables were identified using Least Absolute 
Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression and multivariate logistic regression. A nomogram was constructed 
based on the significant predictors. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic 
curve (AUC), calibration curves, decision curve analysis (DCA), and clinical impact curve (CIC).
Results  Independent predictors of suboptimal remission included BMI > 40 kg/m2, elevated total cholesterol, high neutrophil-
to-lymphocyte ratio, high cortisol, low skeletal muscle index, and elevated visceral-to-subcutaneous adipose tissue area ratio. 
The constructed nomogram demonstrated strong predictive performance, with AUCs of 0.864 and 0.842 in the training and 
external validation cohorts, respectively. Calibration curves indicated excellent agreement between predicted and observed 
outcomes. DCA and CIC confirmed the model’s clinical utility in both cohorts.
Conclusion  The developed nomogram effectively predicts early weight loss outcomes after LSG, supporting targeted perio-
perative management and personalized nutritional interventions.

Introduction
Obesity, characterized by the excessive accumulation of 
body fat, is a chronic metabolic disorder resulting from 
an imbalance between energy intake and expenditure. It is 
associated with various health complications, including type 
2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), hypertension, coronary heart 
disease, and obstructive sleep apnea/hypopnea syndrome 
(OSAHS) [1, 2]. Bariatric and metabolic surgery (BMS) 
has emerged as an effective long-term treatment option for 
obesity, significantly reducing body mass, enhancing life 
expectancy, and alleviating associated inflammatory con-
ditions [3, 4]. Laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG) has 
become the most prevalent bariatric procedure due to its 
superior weight loss outcomes and lower complication rates 
[5, 6]. Traditionally, preoperative body mass index (BMI) 
has been utilized to evaluate the nutritional status of patients 
with obesity and predict postoperative weight loss outcomes 
following BMS [7]. However, studies examining the rela-
tionship between obesity and cardiovascular mortality based 
on BMI have revealed an “obesity paradox,” wherein certain 
patients with obesity and cardiovascular disease demonstrate 
better prognoses than their normal-weight counterparts [8]. 
Consequently, relying solely on BMI may lead to inaccurate 
predictions. Studies have identified factors beyond BMI that 
correlate with early postoperative weight loss outcomes after 
LSG, including age [9], alcohol consumption [10], surgical 
procedure, and preoperative weight loss [11]. Nevertheless, 
because most existing models do not fully utilize objective 
clinical data, they may exhibit certain limitations in clinical 
applications. Based on previous studies, it is expected to 
establish a specific tool for predicting early weight loss out-
comes after LSG. In addition, the variability in early postop-
erative benefits and weight loss among patients with obesity 
necessitates tailored perioperative interventions.
Patients with obesity in this study underwent routine 
clinical assessments, including hematological examina-
tions and abdominal computed tomography (CT) scans, to 
evaluate their health status and exclude malignant diseases. 
Several studies have demonstrated that circulating inflamma-
tory markers can aid in diagnosing chronic diseases and pre-
dict prognoses [12–14]. Given that obesity is characterized 
by chronic systemic inflammation, specific inflammatory 
markers such as the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), 
systemic inflammation response index (SIRI), and systemic 
immune-inflammation index (SII) may help predict early 
weight loss after LSG [15].
Additionally, body composition measurements from CT 
scans have gained traction for assessing nutritional status 
and predicting outcomes related to various diseases [16, 17]. 
Skeletal muscle is a crucial component of body composition, 
and progressive loss of its quality, quantity, and function 
can lead to sarcopenia [18]. Previous studies have estab-
lished strong associations between sarcopenia, metabolic 
syndrome (Met-S), and T2DM [19–22]. In addition, Ibra-
him et al. demonstrated that visceral adipose tissue (VAT) 
cells are more metabolically active, sensitive to lipolysis, 
and insulin resistant than subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT) 
[23]. Studies also indicate a positive correlation between 
visceral adipose tissue area (VATA) and adverse cardiovas-
cular events [24, 25]. Despite these findings, the association 
between CT-based body composition and LSG outcomes 
remains unclear.
We conducted a retrospective study to explore predictive 
factors for suboptimal remission of preoperative weight after 
LSG based on preoperative inflammatory-nutritional indica-
tors and CT-based body composition parameters. The goal 
was to develop a nomogram model to identify patients at risk 
of suboptimal remission, providing a valuable reference for 
clinical decision-making and enhancing long-term outcomes 
for patients with obesity.
Methods
Patients
Patients with obesity undergoing LSG at the Affiliated Hos-
pital of Qingdao University and Qilu Hospital of Shandong 
University (Qingdao) between January 2016 and June 2023 
were retrospectively analyzed.
The inclusion criteria included the following: BMI ≥ 30 
kg/m2, patients aged 18 to 65 years, patients who underwent 
LSG, CT images captured within 1 month preoperatively,

and availability of complete clinical data and postoperative 
follow-up records. The exclusion criteria were as follows: 
occurrence of severe postoperative complications; pregnancy 
within 1 year after surgery; and factors affecting peripheral 
blood counts, including acute or chronic infections, immune 
system diseases, stroke, hematologic neoplasms, myocardial 
infarction, or use of specific medications before treatment. 
A total of 410 patients meeting these criteria were included 
in this study (Fig. 1).
Operation Procedure
All bariatric surgery in the two central institutions is per-
formed by two fixed surgeons.
Data Collection and Follow‑up
Clinical data, inflammatory-nutritional indices, and CT 
images were collected for all patients. Baseline character-
istics included age, sex, BMI, and metabolism-related dis-
eases (T2DM, and hypertension). Measured inflammatory-
nutritional indices included alanine aminotransferase (ALT), 
aspartate aminotransferase (AST), triglycerides (TG), 
total cholesterol (TC), fasting insulin, neutrophils (Neu), 
monocytes, lymphocytes (Lym), and serum albumin (ALB). 
The ratios were computed as follows: NLR = N/L [26], 
SII = P × N/L [14], SIRI = N × M/L, and prognostic nutri-
tional index (PNI) = albumin (g/L) + 5 × L ­(109/L) (where 
N is the neutrophil count, L is the lymphocyte count, M is 
the monocyte count, and P is the platelet count). Patients 
were followed up by telephone or in the outpatient clinic 
at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months postoperatively. Follow-up evalu-
ations included BMI, related hematological examinations, 
and imaging examinations.
Definition of Optimal Early Weight Loss for Patients 
with Obesity
The main outcome was the optimal remission of preopera-
tive weight for LSG patients, defined as a percentage total 
weight loss (%TWL) of ≥ 25 at one year after surgery [27], 
and suboptimal remission was defined as %TWL < 25. 
The %TWL was calculated as follows: %TWL = [(Initial 
weight) − (Postoperative weight)]/(Initial weight) × 100%. 
The initial weight refers to the preoperative weight, and 
the postoperative weight is the weight recorded 1 year after 
LSG.

CT‑Based Body Composition Analysis
Each patient’s body composition was evaluated using SLI-
CEOMATIC software (version 5.0; TomoVision, Magog, 
Canada; http://​www.​tomov​ision.​com; Fig. 2).
A single CT image of the third lumbar vertebra (L3) 
was selected to quantify the body composition component 
characteristics because this anatomical location is strongly 
associated with whole-body volume [28]. By using tissue-
specific attenuation thresholds such as skeletal muscle (− 29 
to 150 Hounsfield unit [HU]), subcutaneous and intramus-
cular adipose tissue (− 190 to − 30 HU), and visceral adi-
pose tissue (− 150 to –50 HU), the VATA, subcutaneous 
adipose tissue area (SATA), intramuscular adipose tissue 
area (IMATA), skeletal muscle area (SMA) (in ­cm2), skeletal 
muscle density (SMD), visceral adipose density (VD), and 
subcutaneous adipose density (SD) (in HU) were depicted 
and measured on cross-sectional images of L3 [29]. The 
total adipose tissue area (TATA) was calculated by adding 
SATA, IMATA, and VATA. The SMA and adipose tissue 
areas were normalized for height in ­m2, giving rise to the 
skeletal muscle index (SMI), visceral adipose tissue index 
(VATI), subcutaneous adipose tissue index (SATI), and total 
adipose tissue index (TATI). Intramuscular adipose tissue 
content (IMAC) was defined as the ratio of SMD (HU) to SD 
(HU) [30]. The visceral to subcutaneous adipose tissue area 
ratio (VSR) was calculated by dividing VATI by SATI [31].

Statistical Analysis
Statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS version 26.0 
(IBM Corp, Armonk, NY, USA) and R (version 4.2.1; R 
Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria).
Intergroup comparisons were conducted using the t-test 
and Mann–Whitney U test. Count data were expressed as 
rates and composition ratios, with intergroup contrasts eval-
uated using the chi-squared (χ2) test or Fisher’s exact test.
The Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator 
(LASSO) regression approach was integrated for dimen-
sionality reduction, identifying optimal predictors while 
minimizing over-fitting [32, 33]. The optimal penalty coef-
ficient for the model was selected based on the lambda 
value corresponding to the cross-validated error within 
one standard deviation of the minimum error. Variables 
filtered by LASSO regression were then subjected to uni-
variate and multivariate logistic regression analyses to 
identify the final predictors and construct a nomogram 
model. Variables with p < 0.05 were regarded as independ-
ent predictors.
Three indicators were used to assess the nomogram dis-
crimination, calibration, and clinical utility. The area under 
the curve (AUC) was used to determine nomogram discrimi-
nation. Calibration curves were used to determine the con-
sistency between the predicted and actual values. Decision 
curve analysis (DCA) and clinical impact curve (CIC) were 
performed to evaluate the clinical usefulness and net ben-
efits of the nomogram. DCA assessed the net benefits of the 
nomogram across different threshold probabilities, determin-
ing its clinical applicability. CIC provided the actual and 
nomogram-predicted numbers of high-risk individuals at 
each threshold probability.
Results
Patient Characteristics
In line with aforementioned criteria, this study included 
410 eligible patients with obesity who underwent LSG 
(Fig. 1), divided into a training set (n = 305) and a valida-
tion set (n = 105). Baseline clinical parameters for both 
groups are shown in Table 1. Most patients were female 
(n = 271), whereas only 139 males were enrolled. Optimal 
remission was achieved by 275 patients (67.1%). 46.1% 
of patients were younger than 30 years of age, and 54.1% 
had a BMI > 40.0 kg/m2. The prevalence rates of T2DM, 
hypertension, and sex hormone abnormalities were 27.6%, 
36.6%, and 29.5%, respectively. There were no significant 
differences between the training and validation sets in early 
weight loss outcomes, inflammatory-nutritional indices, and 
CT-based body composition indices (p > 0.05) (Table 1, 
Table 2).
In addition, compared with the optimal remission group, 
the incidence of T2DM and severe obesity in the suboptimal 
remission group was significantly higher, and cortisol, TC, 
TG, white blood cells, neutrophils, NLR, SIRI, and SII were 
also significantly higher (Table 3). In terms of body com-
position, the incidence of low SMI, high VSR, high VATI, 
high SATI, high TATI, Low SD, and Low VD was higher in 
the suboptimal remission group.
Feature Selection
LASSO and logistic regression models were established 
using the training set. The screening of variables according 
to the lambda values from the LASSO logistic regression 
model is shown in Fig. 3, which presents the LASSO coef-
ficient profiles with non-zero coefficients found using the 
optimal lambda (λ). In this study, λ.1se was chosen, which 
was 0.051, at which point eleven non-zero coefficient vari-
ables were included, namely BMI, TC, Cortisol, NLR, SIRI, 
SII, VSR, SMI, VATI, SATI, and IMATI.
Construction of an Individualized Prediction Model
We performed multivariate logistic regression analysis on 
the variables identified by LASSO regression, and finally 
six independent variables were identified (Table 4). These 
variables were high BMI (odds ratio [OR] = 6.688, 95% 
confidence interval [CI] = 3.249–13.77, p < 0.001), high 
TC (OR = 2.752, 95%CI = 1.461–5.184, p = 0.002), high 
cortisol (OR = 2.323, 95%CI = 1.171–4.610, p = 0.016), 
high NLR (OR = 2.728, 95% CI = 1.424–5.226, p = 0.002), 
high VSR (OR = 4.396, 95% CI = 2.087–9.260, p < 0.001), 
and low SMI (OR = 9.382, 95% CI = 4.571–19.258, 
p < 0.001). Finally, we created a nomogram for opti-
mal remission of weight using these predictive factors 
(Fig. 4).
Model Evaluation
The receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and AUC 
values are depicted in Fig. 5. The AUC of the ROC curve for 
the nomogram was 0.864 (95% CI 0.818–0.910; Fig. 5A) in 
the training set, with a specificity of 78.3% and sensitivity 
of 80.6%. In the validation set, the AUC was 0.842 (95% CI 
0.761–0.923; Fig. 5B), with a specificity of 87.3% and sen-
sitivity of 78.6%. These results demonstrate that the nomo-
gram exhibited relatively good discriminative performance.

DCA and CIC were plotted to evaluate the clinical 
usefulness and applicability of the model. In the DCA, 
the red line represents the net benefit value of the nomo-
gram, while the gray diagonal assumes that all patients 
experienced suboptimal early weight loss, and the black 
line indicates that no patient experienced suboptimal early 
weight loss. Within the threshold range of 0.05 to 0.97 
(abscissa), the DCA of the training cohort showed that 
the net benefit rate (red line) of the prediction model was 
above both extreme lines (black and gray lines), indicating 
that the model had good clinical applicability (Fig. 6C). 
Therefore, the broad threshold range indicates that the 
model has certain clinical value. That is, when the pre-
dicted risk probability of the model exceeds this thresh-
old, the benefit obtained by intervening in patients will be 
greater than the loss. For example, to determine whether 
patients with obesity require surgery, the model can 
compare the predicted postoperative suboptimal weight 
remission risk with the DCA decision threshold to make a 
decision. In addition, when the risk probability predicted 
by the model is low, it may be more appropriate not to 
intervene, that is, obese patients do not undergo surgi-
cal treatment to avoid the side effects and costs of over-
treatment. We have elaborated on the clinical significance 
of AUC values and decision thresholds in the discussion 
section. A similar pattern was observed in the validation 
set, with the nomogram showing greater net benefits com-
pared to the extremes (Fig. 6D).
Clinical impact curve (CIC) analysis was performed in 
Fig. 6 to evaluate clinical applicability of risk prediction 
nomogram. CIC visually showed that the nomogram had 
a superior overall net benefit within the wide and practical 
ranges of threshold probabilities and impacted patient out-
come, which indicates that the model possesses significant 
predictive value (Fig. 6E). Similar results were observed in 
the validation cohorts (Fig. 6F).

Discussion
By 2025, the global prevalence of obesity is projected to 
increase to 18% in men and 21% in women, with severe 
obesity affecting 6% of men and 9% of women [1]. Among 
the surgical options, LSG remains the dominant proce-
dural choice [6]. This study focused on patients with obe-
sity requiring surgical treatment, explored the predictive 
factors, and constructed a predictive model for the effect 
of weight loss in the early postoperative period after LSG 
based on inflammatory-nutritional indicators and CT body 
composition parameters. We highlighted the key factors that 
patients with obesity should consider when undergoing LSG, 
including BMI, hormonal or genetic markers (cortisol),

Traditionally, the percentage of excess weight loss 
(%EWL) has been the standard metric for assessing the effec-
tiveness of post-BMS weight loss. However, recent studies 
suggest an alternative evaluation criterion: %TWL ≥ 25%. 
This measure is superior in predicting optimal early weight 
loss compared to %EWL ≥ 50% [35, 36]. A large cohort 
study of 4497 patients by Arnold et al. showed that the higher 
specificity and sensitivity of %TWL ≥ 25% indicated early 
weight loss effectiveness [35]. Besides, in this study, 82.5% 
of patients achieved %TWL > 20%, of which 58% achieved 
%TWL > 25% at 6 months after surgery, and 68% achieved 
%TWL > 25% at 1 year after surgery. Similarly, Ricard et al. 
found that %TWL is less influenced by preoperative BMI 
and should be the preferred measure for evaluating weight 
loss after BMS [36]. Consequently, we defined optimal early 
weight loss as %TWL ≥ 25% within 1 year postoperatively.
Patients with a BMI exceeding 40 kg/m2 are classified as 
having class III obesity or severe obesity [37, 38]. Our analy-
sis identified BMI as an independent predictor of weight 
loss, with those classified as severe obesity (OR = 3.798, 
p < 0.001) showing a greater likelihood of suboptimal remis-
sion, corroborating findings from other studies [39, 40]. 
Fahad et al. also established that a BMI > 50 kg/m2 is a risk 
factor for BS outcomes [41]. Thus, perioperative interven-
tions are crucial for patients with high preoperative BMI.

Additionally, we identified low SMI and high VSR as inde-
pendent risk factors for suboptimal early weight loss. Previ-
ous studies have documented the predictive value of SMI and 
VSR across various diseases (T2DM, hypertension, Met-S, 
cardiovascular conditions, acute pancreatitis, inflammatory 
bowel disease, and cancer) [53–56]. Priya et al. noted that 
a high VSR correlated with shorter intervals of inflamma-
tory bowel disease flare-ups [53]. Ian et al. posited that VAT 
is associated with dyslipidemia and the atherogenic obesity 
phenotype [55]. Moreover, Cuihong et al. concluded that VAT 
and total adipose tissue (TAT) are strong predictors of Met-S, 
while abdominal skeletal muscle primarily predicts Met-S in 
men [56]. These findings may be attributed to structural and 
functional differences between SAT and VAT [57]. VAT is 
rich in large adipocytes and inflammatory cells [58, 59], and 
is a major source of adiponectin [60], while SAT is the larg-
est source of leptin [61]. In addition, VAT in patients with 
obesity contains more macrophages compared to SAT, and the 
macrophages in VAT proliferate in obesity [62]. VAT has been 
reported to secrete various pro-inflammatory cytokines, such 
as TNF-α, IL-6, and chemokines, and respond more strongly 
to inflammation and apoptosis [63, 64].
This study innovatively explored the relationship between 
the body components including VSR, SMI and VATI, and 
the weight loss of patients with obesity undergoing LSG, 
and the results suggested that VSR and SMI may be the new 
biomarkers for the suboptimal remission of patients with 
obesity. The prediction model based on body composition 
and inflammatory nutrition indicators has good accuracy and 
clinical applicability, which can guide clinical decision-mak-
ing and intervention treatment. Therefore, low SMI and high-
VSR may be the potential therapeutic targets for improving 
the weight loss outcome of patients with obesity after LSG.
We speculate that preoperative nutritional intervention for 
patients with high risk of suboptimal remission can poten-
tially enhance the efficacy of LSG by improving low SMI, 
high VSR, high BMI, and high TC level. For example, resist-
ance training and other exercise interventions combined with 
protein, whey protein, and creatine supplementation can 
increase muscle mass and strength and improve sarcopenia 
in adults [65, 66]. Bifidobacterium animalis can improve 
the intestinal environment and reduce abdominal visceral 
fat [67, 68]. And, patients with obesity may achieve better 
weight loss by maintaining normal TC levels for a long time 
through a low-fat diet and oral lipid-lowering drugs. Patients 
should take appropriate physical exercise before surgery to 
reduce preoperative BMI and VSR as much as possible to 
improve the prognosis. We recommend prolonging post-
operative treatment and intensive follow-up for high-risk 
patients with poor prognosis, such as exercise, nutritional 
therapy, and anti-obesity medications (AOM). In addition, 
the model can compare the predicted risk of postoperative 
suboptimal remission with the DCA decision threshold, and 
then determine whether patients with obesity need surgery.

predictive models. Unlike traditional evaluation metrics such 
as AUC, which focus solely on model accuracy, DCA empha-
sizes the practical impact of the model in clinical decision-
making, specifically the consequences of clinical actions.

decide whether intervention is necessary for patients. The

when the model predicts a low-risk probability, it may be more 
appropriate to avoid intervention, such as not recommending 
surgical treatment for obese patients to prevent unnecessary 
side effects and costs associated with over-treatment.
Age has also been implicated in postoperative weight 
loss, with older age negatively correlating with weight 
loss outcomes [9, 69]. However, this relationship was not 
observed in our study, potentially due to the differences in 
the number, ethnicity, or male/female ratio of study sub-
jects, in postoperative medical support, or in explanatory 
variables selected for multivariable regression analysis. 
Therefore, surgical intervention should be widely recom-
mended for all patients of obesity meeting the surgical 
criteria, particularly for those with complex medical con-
ditions unresponsive to conservative treatments.
Our study has several strengths. First, focusing on LSG 
minimizes the bias related to the variability of different 
BMS techniques. Second, the nomogram permitted con-
tinuous assessment of the probability of achieving optimal 
early weight loss, demonstrating relatively good discrimi-
natory capacity in both the training (AUC: 0.864, 95% CI 
0.818–0.910) and validation sets (AUC: 0.842, 95% CI 
0.761–0.923). Our nomogram utilizes readily obtainable 
objective indicators, such as preoperative inflammatory-
nutritional markers and imaging data, enabling both clini-
cians and patients to understand the potential risk factors. 
This visualization tool provides clinical decision-making, 
allowing targeted perioperative interventions for individu-
als at a higher risk of suboptimal early weight loss.

This study has several limitations. First, the retrospec-
tive design and relatively small sample size may have 
introduced selection or recall biases. Second, the follow-
up period was limited to 1 year, which might have missed 
capturing the nadir of weight loss in some patients. Third, 
the generalizability of the findings to other regions or 
ethnic groups remains uncertain, as the study primarily 
included Asian patients who underwent LSG. Addition-
ally, we did not evaluate certain clinical parameters that 
could influence postoperative weight loss, such as men-
tal health status, alcohol consumption, quality of life, 
and specific hormonal or genetic markers (e.g., leptin, 
ghrelin). In addition, the benefits of BMS extend beyond 
weight loss and often include significant improvements 
in related metabolic syndromes. In addition, the predic-
tive performance of the nomogram in specific populations 
is unknown, such as patients with extremely high BMI 
or specific metabolic profiles. Finally, while focusing on 
postoperative weight loss provided a clear study outcome, 
it also overlooked the broader metabolic improvements 
associated with BMS, including conditions like T2DM, 
OSAHS, and fatty liver disease. Future multicenter pro-
spective studies are required to validate the adaptivity of 
nomogram in diverse population cohorts and to evaluate 
whether additional variables should be incorporated into 
the nomogram.
Inflammatory-nutritional indices and body composition 
measurements can be easily and rapidly obtained through 
preoperative hematological examinations and abdominal 
CT scans, without incurring significant additional costs for 
patients or healthcare providers. The model developed in 
this study assists clinicians in evaluating the likelihood of 
suboptimal remission of preoperative weight after LSG, 
thereby informing personalized treatment strategies to 
improve postoperative outcomes.
Conclusions
Our results indicate that CT-based body composition param-
eters and inflammatory nutritional markers, notably BMI, 
TC, cortisol, NLR, VSR, and SMI, are correlated with early 
weight loss outcomes following LSG in obese patients. The 
nomogram developed based on these indicators effectively 
predicted weight loss outcomes and demonstrated robust

clinical decision-making and supporting the development 
of personalized perioperative treatment plans, particularly 
for early interventions targeting patients at higher risk for 
suboptimal weight loss.

Abstract: Purpose Laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG) is an effective treatment for obesity, but early weight loss outcomes vary owing to individual nutritional and metabolic differences. We developed a nomogram model to predict early weight loss after LSG, incorporating computed tomography (CT)-based body composition metrics and preoperative inflammatory- nutritional markers. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 305 patients with obesity who underwent LSG at the Affiliated Hospital of Qingdao University between January 2016 and June 2023. An external validation cohort of 105 patients from a separate institution was also included. Patients were categorized into optimal remission (%total weight loss [%TWL] ≥ 25%) and suboptimal remis- sion (%TWL < 25%) weight loss groups one year postoperatively. Predictive variables were identified using Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression and multivariate logistic regression. A nomogram was constructed based on the significant predictors. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration curves, decision curve analysis (DCA), and clinical impact curve (CIC). Results Independent predictors of suboptimal remission included BMI > 40 kg/m2, elevated total cholesterol, high neutrophil- to-lymphocyte ratio, high cortisol, low skeletal muscle index, and elevated visceral-to-subcutaneous adipose tissue area ratio. The constructed nomogram demonstrated strong predictive performance, with AUCs of 0.864 and 0.842 in the training and external validation cohorts, respectively. Calibration curves indicated excellent agreement between predicted and observed outcomes. DCA and CIC confirmed the model’s clinical utility in both cohorts. Conclusion The developed nomogram effectively predicts early weight loss outcomes after LSG, supporting targeted perio- perative management and personalized nutritional interventions.
